chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding

the fasting one who performs ablution for the prayer, so water enters his throat. He said: If his ablution was for an obligatory prayer, there is nothing upon him; and if his ablution was for an optional prayer, he must make it up.
ai.seo_question: Does water entering the throat during wudu break the fast of a Shia Muslim?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the juristic distinction between obligatory (fard) and optional (nafl) prayers regarding the validity of the fast when water inadvertently enters the throat during wudu. In Shia fiqh, this ruling underscores the principle that minor, unintentional acts during the performance of a mandatory prayer do not invalidate the fast, whereas the same act during a voluntary prayer necessitates making up the fast (qada). This reflects the broader scholarly emphasis on intentionality and the specific context of worship in determining legal consequences.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> regarding the Fasting one performing ablution for the Prayer, so the water enters into his throat. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If his ablution was for the Obligatory Prayer, so there is nothing upon him, but if his ablution was for an optional Prayer, so upon him is the making up for it’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Hammad who has said the following: “I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about

a man who takes wudu’ (ablution) and water enters in his throat. He (the Imam) said, ‘If his wudu’ (ablution) is for an obligatory Salat (prayer) there is not anything on him, but if it is for an optional Salat (prayer); he is required to make its Qada’ (compensatory fast).”’
